_comment: One complete point of view on running data and AI in an enterprise. No company or vendor names. Each chapter is a list of blocks; block types: p, list, table, cards, layers, steps, tiers, timeline, callout.
thesis: My job is not to turn a company into an AI company. It is to make data and AI a multiplier for the company it already wants to become.

principles.title: Start from the business's core learning problem
principles.text: Every business has one quantity whose improvement compounds: yield, forecast accuracy, cycle time, first-pass quality. AI earns its budget by moving that number.

principles.title: Data is an enterprise asset, not an IT by-product
principles.text: Every critical domain needs a named owner, measurable quality, discoverability and accountable stewardship.

principles.title: Context is the moat; models are a commodity
principles.text: Anyone can rent a frontier model. The scarce asset is trusted, permissioned, versioned context an agent can act on.

principles.title: The platform makes the second team faster than the first
principles.text: Any capable group can ship one solution. A platform justifies itself when the fifth team ships in a fraction of the first team's effort.

principles.title: Autonomy is earned per workflow
principles.text: It is never a setting you switch on. The tier is set by how reversible an action is and what a wrong one costs.

principles.title: Govern by design, so the safe path is the fast path
principles.text: Identity, guardrails, policy and logging live in the platform, not in a committee at the end.

principles.title: Evaluation is the product, not the QA step
principles.text: The difference between a demo and a capability is that someone can tell you, on demand, whether it still works.

principles.title: Every answer has a token bill
principles.text: Most of it is avoidable. The harness matters more than the horsepower.

principles.title: Central standards, federated delivery
principles.text: Do once, centrally, what must be identical. Leave with the domains what needs proximity. Write the line down.

principles.title: Measure decisions changed and value created
principles.text: Not models built, pilots run or people trained. If Finance would not sign the number, it is not a result.

chapters.title: Strategy & value
chapters.lead: Enterprises rarely need a parallel AI organization sitting beside the business. They need a small capability that makes every existing team measurably faster at what it already does. The test for any initiative: does it make an existing team's job easier, or does it add one more layer to manage?

blocks.text: The flywheel I am trying to start

items.title: Trusted data
items.text: Owned domains with measured quality.

items.title: Reusable data products and context
items.text: Defined once, used by every team.

items.title: Shared AI platform
items.text: Gateway, evaluation, agents and paved paths.

items.title: Better employee and customer experiences
items.text: Answers inside the tools people already use.

items.title: Faster decisions and innovation
items.text: Cycle time, quality and cost move.

items.title: More value, learning and adoption
items.text: Which feeds richer data back into the loop.

blocks.text: How I choose what goes first

A portfolio is a sequencing problem, not a wish list. The first capabilities set precedent, so they need to be the ones most likely to succeed and most likely to build the shared foundations everything else depends on. I score candidates on four filters.

items.title: High volume
items.text: Enough repetitions a year that a small per-transaction gain compounds into something worth the engineering.

items.title: Document-bound
items.text: The work is reading, extracting and deciding from text and records, which is where current models are strongest.

items.title: Rules exist
items.text: There is a policy, playbook or standard to point to, so correctness can be checked rather than debated.

items.title: Reversible
items.text: A wrong output is caught and corrected cheaply. Irreversible processes wait until the platform has a track record.

blocks.text: Alongside those near-term wins I always hold one bet on the core learning problem: a model inside the physical or scientific loop that removes cycles altogether. That is where the largest value sits, and it is the work my research career prepared me for.
The value case: what I will and will not claim

head: I will report
I will not report
rows: Cost per transaction before and after, with Finance agreeing the baseline
Hours saved multiplied by a loaded rate, presented as cash
Cycle time measured end to end, not just for the automated step
Headcount reductions not agreed with the leader who owns that headcount
Straight-through processing and exception rates, trended
Revenue attributed to a productivity tool
Capacity redeployed, named by team and role
Pilot results extrapolated to enterprise scale without a scaled measurement

blocks.text: One inflated benefit claim that fails an audit costs more credibility than three honest quarters earn. I would rather report a smaller verified number than a larger arguable one.

chapters.title: Data foundation
chapters.lead: Most AI disappointment traces back to data, not models. So no model work starts until the data it depends on is owned, defined and measured.

blocks.text: Ownership with names attached

items.title: Owner
items.text: A business leader accountable for the domain's data and for hitting its quality targets.

items.title: Steward
items.text: Owns definitions, business rules and the glossary for the domain.

items.title: Custodian
items.text: Owns the pipelines, access controls and operational health of the data.

blocks.text: One pipeline, three layers of trust

items.title: Sources
items.text: ERP, MES, CRM, PLM, historians, documents and sensors.

items.title: Bronze
items.text: Raw ingest, immutable and replayable.

items.title: Silver
items.text: Cleansed and conformed against the quality framework.

items.title: Gold
items.text: Curated data products with owners and contracts.

items.title: Catalog & lineage
items.text: Meaning is looked up, not inferred, from source column to decision.

items.title: Agents & decisions
items.text: Analytics, models and agents consume Gold through the context layer.

blocks.text: Quality you can see

head: Dimension
The question it answers
rows: Completeness
Are the required fields and records present?
Conformance
Does the data follow standards, formats, units and plausible ranges?
Consistency
Does the same business object mean the same thing in every system?
Accuracy & integrity
Do values reflect physical reality, and do relationships hold?
Timeliness & alignment
Is it fresh enough for the decision, and aligned in time across sensors and systems?

blocks.text: I track coverage in two directions: whether a standard exists for a domain, and whether it is actually in use at every site and system. "We have a standard" and "the standard is used everywhere" are different claims, and federation succeeds or fails on the second.
No model before the data is ready
Every use case earns a data readiness score, technical and business, before development starts.

head: Technical readiness
Business readiness
rows: Quality measured on the five dimensions
Every term the use case depends on is defined, owned and approved
Named owner, steward and custodian
The process is documented and mapped to its data
Column-level lineage from source to decision
The decision is mapped: who makes it today and what will change
Every Gold metric has a definition, unit, logic, valid range and owner
A named business owner and a measured baseline exist
Access rights and retention are clear
Legal basis, training and procedure updates are planned

blocks.text: Data quality is also an economics lever. Once meaning is looked up rather than inferred, every downstream model call spends fewer tokens working out what the data means.

chapters.title: Context & knowledge
chapters.lead: The context layer is where a company's advantage actually lives. Models change every few months; decades of operating records, designs, procedures and expert know-how do not.

items.title: A semantic layer
items.text: Business definitions fixed once, so "yield", "on-time" or "active customer" mean one thing to every person and every agent.

items.title: Retrieval beyond vectors
items.text: Vector, graph and structured retrieval together. Many enterprise questions are relational, and graphs are the natural shape for lineage, networks and dependencies.

items.title: Entitlements inherited from source
items.text: An agent can never surface data the requesting person could not open directly. Permissions travel with the data.

items.title: Lineage and provenance
items.text: Every answer traces to the record that produced it, which is also how AI-assisted work earns a defensible audit trail.

blocks.text: Three levels of return

items.title: Level 1 · Productivity
items.text: Specifications, procedures, design rules and quality records become discoverable and reusable.

items.title: Level 2 · Innovation speed
items.text: New projects start from approved context, data products and components instead of rebuilding them.

items.title: Level 3 · New products
items.text: Trusted context can eventually power customer-facing services. A strategic option, validated before it is committed.

blocks.text: Tacit knowledge deserves its own program. In plants and labs the most valuable know-how lives in experienced people. Capturing it as structured guidance, with their names on it, both protects the company and gives those experts the recognition they rarely get.

chapters.title: AI platform
chapters.lead: Seven layers, each with one owner and one reason to exist. A layer belongs in the center only if doing it once, identically, is clearly better than doing it many times in context.

items.title: Domain solutions
items.text: Built by domain teams on the paved path. Use-case selection, workflow redesign and domain evaluation criteria stay close to the work.

items.title: Golden paths
items.text: Scaffolds, SDKs, reference apps, release gates and templates for each authority tier. This is the product the platform team actually sells.

items.title: Evaluation & observability
items.text: Golden datasets, regression gates, tracing, drift watch and continuous production sampling.

items.title: Agent runtime & orchestration
items.text: Tool registry, planning and memory, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, rollback and a tested kill switch.

items.title: Model gateway
items.text: One path to every model: routing and fallback, caching, policy and PII filters, cost attribution per team.

items.title: Context
items.text: Semantic layer, vector, graph and structured retrieval, inherited entitlements, lineage. The moat.

items.title: Data estate
items.text: Operational, engineering, commercial and enterprise data, delivered as governed data products.

blocks.text: Governance spans every layer rather than sitting as a gate at the end. Cybersecurity, enterprise architecture, legal and finance are partners in the design, not reviewers of the result.
The gateway is the control point

items.title: Control
items.text: Policy enforcement, PII and trade-secret filters, logging, data-residency routing and per-request identity. One place to change a rule and one place to prove it was applied.

items.title: Economics
items.text: Cost attributed to the requesting team on every call, routing by task class, semantic caching and budget alerts. Finance sees a real bill by domain.

items.title: Optionality
items.text: Provider abstraction, so a workload can move between model vendors or clouds as prices and terms change. Negotiating leverage becomes a design property.

blocks.text: Retrofitting a gateway after eighteen months of direct model calls is a year of painful work. A gateway that only routes, logs and attributes cost is worth more in month two than a complete platform in month nine, because it starts producing the usage data that tells you what to build next.
The golden path, end to end

items.title: Intake · 1 week
items.text: A one-page business case: the workflow, the decision changed, the baseline, the named owner, the authority tier and the data. No production owner, no start.

items.title: Scaffold · day one
items.text: A repository that already works, with gateway auth, approved retrieval, tracing, an evaluation stub and CI. The first commit is domain logic.

items.title: Evaluate · continuous
items.text: No golden dataset, no promotion. Domains write the criteria; the platform runs the harness and regression gates on every change.

items.title: Review · 3 days
items.text: One parallel review of security, privacy, responsible AI and architecture against a published checklist scaled to the tier.

items.title: Deploy
items.text: Production means operated: a named owner, on-call, dashboards for quality, latency and cost, and a documented rollback.

items.title: Measure · 30/90/180 days
items.text: The intake baseline is re-measured with Finance. Capabilities that miss their threshold are fixed or retired.

head: Step a builder faces
Without a paved path
On the golden path
rows: Get model access
Open a vendor account, wait on legal, manage keys locally
One gateway credential, already reviewed
Reach trustworthy data
Find a source, negotiate access, re-implement permissions
Registered context sources with entitlements and lineage

blocks.text: The commitment I publish: intake decisions in five working days, a scaffold the day a use case is approved, combined review in three days for lower tiers. A central function that is slow and mandatory is worse than none, so if we miss, domains get a documented exception path.
Physical AI and digital twins

For operations-heavy businesses the platform extends into simulation. A physics-grounded digital twin of a plant, line or fleet becomes a place to test schedules, layouts and maintenance strategies before touching the real world, and a conversational layer lets planners query it in plain language. Physics stays in the loop: thermal limits, capacity constraints and degradation curves bound what a model may say, and hybrid physics-ML beats either alone when failure data is thin.

chapters.title: Agentic systems
chapters.lead: Autonomy is not a property of the technology. It is a permission granted per workflow, set by two questions: how reversible is the action, and how expensive is a wrong one?

items.title: Assist
items.may: Retrieve, summarize, draft and explain. Output goes to a person who decides what to do with it.
items.control: The human is the actor. The agent never writes anywhere.
items.evidence: Golden dataset, citation to source on every claim, light security review, usage telemetry.

items.title: Propose
items.may: Prepare a complete action, such as a plan change, a case response or a document, and stage it for approval.
items.control: Explicit human approval before anything commits, logged with the reasoning shown.
items.evidence: Everything in T1, plus approval and override rates and a review of what humans corrected.

items.title: Act within bounds
items.may: Execute inside declared limits on value, scope and time. Escalate anything outside them.
items.control: Bounds enforced in the runtime, not the prompt. Kill switch and one-step rollback are mandatory.
items.evidence: Everything in T2, plus shadow mode until agreement with humans clears a threshold, a full audit trail and sampled human review.

items.title: Operate
items.may: Own a recurring process end to end and report by exception.
items.control: A named executive is accountable. Dual control on irreversible steps. Formal change management.
items.evidence: Sustained T3 performance, a documented failure-mode analysis, and sign-off from the business owner, legal and cybersecurity.

blocks.text: The rules that make tiers real

items: The tier is declared at intake and enforced by the runtime, not asserted in a design document.
Tiers are earned, not assigned. Nothing launches above T2, and promotion requires evidence from live operation.
Every agent has one named human owner who is accountable for its behavior and reachable when it misbehaves.
Anything touching regulatory submissions, safety, product release or contractual commitments stays at T2 by default, however good the model gets.
The kill switch is tested. An untested rollback is not a rollback.

blocks.text: Four patterns worth standardizing

items.title: Grounded answer
items.text: Retrieve, ground, answer, cite. The workhorse. Measure retrieval quality, not just the answer.

items.title: Structured extraction
items.text: Document to schema with confidence scores and a human queue for low-confidence fields. The highest near-term return in most enterprises.

items.title: Tool-using workflow
items.text: Plan, call registered tools, check results, escalate. Tools are registered and permissioned centrally, never ad hoc.

items.title: Monitor and escalate
items.text: Watch a stream, detect a condition, raise a case with the evidence attached.

blocks.text: What I would not do: build a multi-agent architecture because it is interesting. Most enterprise problems are one well-grounded model with good retrieval and a clean tool interface. Multi-agent designs multiply failure modes, cost and debugging effort, and should be used only where a single agent has demonstrably failed.

chapters.title: Governance, risk & responsible AI
chapters.lead: Speed and control only conflict when governance is a committee. When it is written standards plus automated enforcement, both come from the same place.

blocks.text: What "production-ready" means, written down

head: Requirement
The bar
How it is enforced
rows: Validation
A golden dataset with domain-written criteria, scored above an agreed threshold, with a regression gate on every model, prompt or retrieval change
Automated in CI; a failing gate blocks promotion
Traceability
Every output traceable to the sources and tool calls that produced it, retained as long as legal requires
Tracing on by default; absence fails the gate
Monitoring
Live quality, latency, cost, usage and escalation dashboards with alert owners
Provisioned by the platform at deploy
Ownership
A named technical owner, a named business owner, an on-call path and a tested rollback
Recorded in the service registry; no owner, no production
Risk management
Declared tier, runtime-enforced bounds, documented failure modes, a review cadence matched to the tier
Enforced by the runtime, reviewed at tier depth
Entitlements
The system never surfaces data the user could not access directly
Inherited from source at the context layer

blocks.text: Risk-tier every model, not just every agent

A meeting summarizer and a model that sets a process parameter, prices a contract or informs a regulatory filing do not deserve the same review. Higher tiers get locked model versions, formal change control, independent validation by people outside the build line, and drift monitoring with management-of-change when the process shifts. Lower tiers get a light, fast path. Proportion is what lets the organization move quickly where it is safe.
Anchored in recognized frameworks

head: Framework
How I use it
rows: NIST AI RMF and its Generative AI Profile
The organizing structure: govern, map, measure, manage
ISO/IEC 42001
The target AI management system, with certification readiness as an option where customers need evidence
ISO/IEC 23894
The AI risk-assessment method
EU AI Act
Applied wherever operations reach the EU; most industrial uses are not high-risk, but HR and employment uses can be
OWASP LLM and agentic guidance, MITRE ATLAS
Threat taxonomy for red-teaming
NIST CSF 2.0, SP 800-53, IEC 62443
Cyber and OT controls owned by security, with AI controls mapped onto them

blocks.text: The frameworks converge on four things: risk-based classification, transparency, meaningful human oversight and accountability. Every higher-tier review also asks three ethical questions: how serious could the harm be, who is most vulnerable, and who holds responsibility?
A short policy stack and a few clear forums

items.title: Policy stack
items.text: AI policy and principles; acceptable use; risk classification; data for AI; model and agent lifecycle; third-party AI; AI incident response.

items.title: Steering committee · quarterly
items.text: Strategy, risk appetite, funding and the highest-tier approvals, with internal audit observing.

items.title: Governance council · bi-weekly
items.text: Lower-tier approvals, policy, exceptions and incidents, with security, legal, privacy and data governance.

items.title: Data council and site champions · monthly
items.text: Standards, glossary, quality targets and data contracts; adoption, feedback and intake from the front line.

blocks.text: Risks I treat as first-class

items: Intellectual property and trade secrets: contractual and technical guarantees that no vendor trains on company data, and classification-aware routing so the most sensitive material reaches only approved deployments.
Regulatory and claims exposure: anything that could become a submission or a public claim stays human-approved with full traceability, indefinitely.
Data residency and cross-border transfer: the gateway routes by data classification and jurisdiction, because asking each team to get it right is not a control.
Entitlement leakage: zero tolerance, measured and reported.

chapters.title: Economics of AI
chapters.lead: Enterprise AI programs rarely fail on capability. They stall when unit economics turn out to be indefensible at scale: a per-query cost that was invisible for forty pilot users becomes a line item someone has to defend for four thousand.

blocks.text: Where the money actually goes

items.title: Context bloat
items.text: Stuffing everything retrievable into the window because it is easier than retrieving well. Usually the largest avoidable line.

items.title: Over-powered routing
items.text: Sending classification and extraction to a frontier model because it was the scaffold default.

items.title: Retry and loop waste
items.text: Agents that re-plan on ambiguity instead of escalating. Cost grows non-linearly.

items.title: No caching
items.text: The same questions answered from scratch hundreds of times a day.

blocks.text: The optimization ladder

head: Move
What changes
Cost to implement
rows: Retrieval discipline
Rank and trim context to what the task needs; often better accuracy too
Low
Task-class routing
Small models for classification and extraction, frontier models only for open reasoning
Low once the gateway exists
Semantic caching
Near-duplicate questions served from cache with freshness rules
Moderate
Batch versus interactive
Anything not waiting on a person moves to scheduled batch
Low
Distillation
A small model trained on a large one's traces for a narrow, stable, high-volume task
High; justified only at real volume

blocks.text: The harness matters more than the horsepower. A cheap model that starts with company context, the right skill pack and clean tools routinely beats an expensive model that has to research what the company is on every call.
What I report every month

items: Cost per outcome by capability, trended: the headline number
Spend by domain, attributed at the gateway and reconciled with Finance
Cache hit rate, and the spend it avoided
Routing mix by model class, with drift flagged
Idle capability spend: what we pay for things nobody uses

blocks.text: Build, buy and partner

Partners accelerate work we have specified; they never define the architecture. Anything load-bearing, such as the gateway, the evaluation harness and the context layer, is owned by employees, whoever writes the first version. Every vendor faces three tests: can we leave within two quarters, does the contract prohibit training on our data, and does using it deepen our own team's capability or replace it?

chapters.title: Organization & talent
chapters.lead: The org chart is a leverage question, not a staffing question. A deliberately small central core owns what must be done once; embedded practitioners sit with the business; an independent function validates the highest-risk models.

items.title: Embedded pods
items.text: Close to the decision. Data scientists and AI engineers sit with operations, supply chain, R&D, commercial and finance, with a business owner setting priorities and measuring value.

items.title: Central platform & methods
items.text: Built once, used everywhere: platform engineering, evaluation and operations, architecture and governance.

items.title: Independent validation
items.text: A small model-risk function that validates the highest-tier models and reports outside the build line, so the organization never grades its own work.

blocks.text: Who decides what

head: Role
Decides
rows: Business domains
Which use cases are worth doing, what good output looks like, whether to accept the residual risk of a tier, when a capability stops being worth operating
Data & AI leadership
Architecture and the paved path, the production bar and release gates, model routing and cost controls, what is built centrally versus federated
Executive sponsor
Ambition and risk appetite, funding, cross-business trade-offs, the highest-tier authorizations
Security, legal, risk
Enterprise controls, the operational-technology boundary, regulatory interpretation

blocks.text: What each side owes the other

head: The core owes the domains
The domains owe the core
rows: An intake decision in 5 days
A named production owner
A working scaffold the same day
An agreed baseline
Review in 3 days
Evaluation criteria for their workflow
Published standards, working examples and a person who answers
Use of the paved path, or a documented exception

blocks.text: Talent: the part only a leader can do

items.title: Hire deliberately mixed profiles
items.text: Statisticians and forecasters, optimization specialists, ML and GenAI engineers who ship, and domain engineers who want to model.

items.title: Grow on a real technical ladder
items.text: Principal and distinguished tracks that pay as well as management, so the best scientists keep doing science.

items.title: Rotate for domain fluency
items.text: Embedded practitioners spend two or three quarters in a domain, then return to the core with what they learned. Patterns that work become part of the paved path.

items.title: Four competency tracks
items.text: Platform engineering, applied AI engineering, AI product management, and evaluation and operations, each with levelled expectations and portfolio-based promotion.

items.title: One hiring bar
items.text: Structured hiring and performance management across every location, the same process I built from zero at a startup and run today across two countries.

items.title: Literacy beyond the team
items.text: Analysts, engineers and leaders across the business learn to frame a decision, read a forecast interval and question a model.

chapters.title: Change & adoption
chapters.lead: Adoption is earned, not mandated. If someone can get an answer faster by going around the platform, they will, and they should. That is a defect report about the platform.

items.title: Capacity, not cuts
items.text: The goal is fewer repetitive tasks, faster decisions and more room for engineering, customer and creative work. Where workforce change is genuinely needed, the answer is transparency, reskilling and redeployment, not a promise that technology never affects jobs.

items.title: Teams move up the stack
items.text: Existing BI and analytics teams are developed, not displaced. They move from one-off reports to building the reusable data products and agentic tools everyone else uses.

items.title: Treat internal users as customers
items.text: Design for the person doing the work, not the reporting layer. A tool that costs a frontline user time will be abandoned by week three, whatever the mandate says.

items.title: Earn trust before asking for it
items.text: Start with grounded, cited assistance. Never ask an expert to trust a model whose failure modes you cannot explain. Experts forgive a model that is uncertain and never forgive one that is confidently wrong.

items.title: A literacy ladder open to everyone
items.text: AI fluency is a company-wide ladder anyone can climb, not a perk for a technical elite.

items.title: Listening before pitching
items.text: The first month is a listening tour on the floor, in the lab and with the field teams. I am the AI leader in the room, not the domain expert.

blocks.text: One front door

Getting an answer today often means knowing which system holds the data, which analyst owns it, whether a dashboard exists and whom to ask if it does not. The end state is one governed front door, inside each person's existing permissions, that composes an answer or a live view from approved data products rather than a one-off chat reply. It is also the single best lever on cost, because every call starts warm with the right context.

chapters.title: The first 90 days and first year
chapters.lead: A 30/60/90-day plan, then three quarters to prove, widen and industrialize. The first thirty days are weighted toward listening and toward the domain knowledge I do not yet have: architecture can be proposed quickly, but understanding how the business actually runs cannot.

items.title: Listen and inventory
items.text: Structured conversations with executives, domain leaders and platform owners; early engagement with security, legal, architecture and finance so they shape the standards rather than review them. Time on the floor, in the lab and in the field. A full inventory of every AI initiative: cost, owner and whether it is really in production.
items.out: A written baseline and a shortlist of lighthouse use cases with named owners.

items.title: Decide and publish
items.text: Platform architecture agreed. The production-ready definition and authority tiers drafted with security, legal and compliance, then published. Gateway build started. Team design confirmed and first hires opened. Two lighthouse use cases selected, with baselines agreed in writing with Finance.
items.out: Published standards, an agreed roadmap, a funded plan, two use cases in build.

items.title: Ship something real
items.text: Gateway live with routing, logging and cost attribution, plus a migration plan for existing direct model use. Golden path v1. The first lighthouse in production with a named owner, dashboards and a measured baseline. The first monthly value and cost report.
items.out: A working platform with one real capability on it.

items.title: Prove the path
items.text: Second lighthouse in production. All new AI work uses the gateway. Embedded practitioners deployed. Review service levels published and reported. Competency model released. First 90-day value re-measurement.

items.title: Widen
items.text: Every priority area has at least one production capability. Cost-per-outcome trends reported. The first rotation completes and its lessons join the paved path. Vendor strategy formalized under the two-quarter exit test.

items.title: Industrialize
items.text: Reuse rate becomes a reported metric. The first capabilities are retired for missing their value threshold, a sign of health. The year-two roadmap is built with domain leaders, not for them.

blocks.text: What year one should prove

items: A platform every team uses because it is the fastest route, with a pilot-to-production rate I can state as a number.
A benefits register agreed with Finance, with baselines captured before launch and a figure I will defend line by line.
A production bar enforced in the release gate, zero entitlement violations, and security, legal and compliance calling themselves co-authors.
A reported, rising reuse rate and a retired-capabilities list that is not empty.
A lean team on a published competency model, with internal candidates filling senior roles.

chapters.title: The scorecard
chapters.lead: Model count, pilot count and people trained are activity metrics. They tell a leadership team nothing about whether the investment was worth making. This is the scorecard I would run, and expect to be held to.

blocks.text: Reporting is short enough to be read: one page monthly on value, cost, adoption, reliability and risk; a quarterly portfolio review of what is being promoted and what is being retired.

The uncomfortable metric: capabilities retired for missing their value threshold. If that number is zero after a year, either the thresholds are not real or nobody is checking. I report it deliberately.

chapters.title: What I would not do
chapters.lead: These are the commitments that are easy to make on day one and hard to keep in month eight, when something is behind and a shortcut is available. I want them held against me.

items.title: Build a shadow delivery organization
items.text: A central team that competes with domain teams ends up owning a portfolio it cannot operate. The platform's product is the paved path.

items.title: Start a pilot without a production owner
items.text: The pilot graveyard is filled with pilots nobody was ever going to run. Saying no early is worth more than the pilot.

items.title: Grant autonomy before evaluation exists
items.text: No agent acts without a golden dataset, a measured threshold, a tested rollback and a named owner.

items.title: Accept lock-in for short-term speed
items.text: If we cannot leave within two quarters, it is a strategy commitment, not a tool choice, and it goes to the executive sponsor.

items.title: Chase a model zoo
items.text: Supporting every new model and framework is a maintenance tax. A small approved set, reviewed on a schedule.

items.title: Overstate the value
items.text: No hours-times-rate arithmetic presented as cash and no pilot results extrapolated to the enterprise.

items.title: Centralize domain judgment
items.text: What counts as a good answer in a domain is the domain's call. The moment the center defines it, the standards stop being trusted.

items.title: Hire ahead of the operating model
items.text: Twenty people without a paved path produce twenty bespoke solutions. Run light, then hire into a structure that makes each person more effective.
